blocks.text: Austria had no colonies, or did it? The Habsburg Empire came close to building a colonial empire several times, and each time it failed. When we think of colonialism, we picture Britain or France, powers that carved up Africa, Asia, and the Americas. But Austria?

The Habsburgs never held a large, unified colonial empire in the classic sense. Still, over the centuries, they had colonial possessions and ambitions, and the story of how those efforts collapsed says a lot about the limits of Austrian power. The Habsburgs actually did rule a global empire once, but it fell apart. Under Emperor Charles V in the sixteenth century, they controlled a vast realm on which the sun never set.

Charles inherited the Austrian and Burgundian lands from his father, Philip, and the Spanish and southern Italian territories from his mother, Joanna. This was the age of discovery, and the Habsburgs possessed the so-called Spanish colonial empire, centered on Latin and South America. Charles V controlled the territories seized by the Spanish conquistadors, as well as parts of Southeast Asia, including the Philippines, which were later named after his son Philip. But calling the Spanish overseas territories “colonies” is historically and legally imprecise. These lands were not considered foreign possessions. They were integral parts of the Spanish Crown, described more accurately as viceroyalties or territories of the Kingdom of Castile. So what exactly is the difference between a colony and a dependent territory? The term “colony” comes from the Latin “colere,” meaning to cultivate or farm. In modern times, a colony referred to a foreign, dependent territory of a state, lacking its own political and economic power. After the conquest, the American territories were incorporated into the Crown of Castile not as colonies but as kingdoms. The indigenous peoples were legally considered vassals of the Spanish king, not rightless colonial subjects. Administration was handled not by a colonial trading company but by viceroys who directly represented the king in Spain, much like the administration of European provinces.

There was also a strong drive for religious integration, bringing the indigenous population into the Catholic Church and under the Spanish crown, a goal that went beyond mere economic exploitation. These details might sound minor, but they explain why Austria officially had no colonies at that time. Nevertheless, the territories were economically dependent on the exploitation of raw materials like gold and silver, which is why historians still commonly use the term “Spanish colonial empire. ” The vast empire was eventually divided between the Austrian and Spanish lines of the Habsburgs, and the overseas territories stayed with the Spanish line until 1700, when the last Spanish Habsburg died and the War of the Spanish Succession broke out. With their defeat in that war, the Habsburgs lost not only Spain but all their overseas possessions. Suddenly, they were no longer globally connected, and they faced significant disadvantages in overseas trade. In the eighteenth century, Austria actively sought to participate in the lucrative overseas commerce, but Great Britain, Denmark, Portugal, Spain, France, and the Netherlands were far ahead. In 1722, Emperor Charles VI founded the Imperial East India Company in the Austrian Netherlands, in what is now Belgium. The company maintained trading posts in India and China and generated surprisingly good profits. However, under pressure primarily from England and the Netherlands, it had to be dissolved in 1731. Those powers did not want an additional competitor on the Asian trading stage, and the British offered to sign the Pragmatic Sanction in return. That law, among other things, enabled Charles’s daughter Maria Theresa to later assume power in Austria.

Maria Theresa succeeded her father not only on the Austrian throne but also in his colonial ambitions. She founded an East India Company in Trieste, one of the Habsburgs’ most important ports. From 1776, its ships sailed under the imperial flag of Habsburg-Lorraine, commanded by the Dutchman William Bolt, who had previously worked for the British East India Company. Between 1778 and 1783, there was a short-lived attempt to establish the Nicobar Islands in the Indian Ocean as an Austrian colony. Although Denmark had claimed the Nicobar Islands, in 1778 the ships of the Trieste Trading Company acquired several of them from the local inhabitants, and one was even named after Maria Theresa, “Teressa. ” The islands were officially declared Austrian crown colonies, and new trading posts were established on the Malabar Coast of India. Yet as early as 1785, under Danish pressure, the Austrian occupiers were forced to leave the islands. Attention then turned to East Africa.

In March 1777, the trading company’s ships reached Delagoa Bay, now Maputo Bay in Mozambique on the southeast coast of Africa. Through treaties with local rulers, they acquired, among other things, the exclusive right of first refusal for ivory. The colony in Delagoa subsequently exported approximately seventy-five thousand pounds of ivory annually. A small fortification with a garrison of ten men was built and declared an Austrian colony before the ships sailed on toward India.

However, the bay was lost to Portugal as early as 1781. For the first time, Austria had genuine colonies, and it lost them almost as quickly. In 1783, under pressure from the naval powers and lacking a comparable navy of its own to protect the colonies, Maria Theresa’s successor, Joseph I, dissolved the Trieste Trading Company. The Nicobar Islands and Delagoa Bay were lost, and Habsburg colonial policy in the eighteenth century came to an end. But it resurfaced later. In the nineteenth century, the Austrian Navy once again undertook several voyages of discovery, which also served to explore opportunities for colonial expansion. In 1802, the Austrian West African Maritime Trading Company was founded in Vienna, with the goal of trade and influence in West Africa. Emperor Franz II granted the company an exclusive trading privilege for a full twenty-five years. As early as 1803, a ship set sail from the port of Trieste. On board were merchants, explorers, and the hope of new trading posts, called trading houses, and perhaps even a colony of their own. But when the ship returned, Europe was in chaos. The wars against Napoleon made any further expansion impossible.

Another colonial dream had failed. In the second half of the nineteenth century came one of the greatest adventures in Austrian history: the Novara Expedition. In 1857, the frigate Novara set sail from Trieste on a circumnavigation of the globe, but here too there were colonial plans. One of the voyage’s destinations was once again the Nicobar Islands. Austria considered taking over the archipelago as a colony. In 1858, the Novara reached the islands, but ultimately nothing happened. No occupation, no flag was raised. Instead, the ship returned in 1859 with a wealth of scientific discoveries. A triumph for research, but not for colonial ambitions. Yet they did not give up. One more expedition was meant to bring territorial gains: the North Pole Expedition. In 1872, Austria-Hungary embarked on a completely different adventure.

An expedition set sail for the North Pole aboard the ship Admiral Tegethoff. But there were difficulties. The ship remained trapped in the pack ice for over a year. Finally, some men reached an unknown group of islands on foot across the ice. They named it Franz Joseph Land and raised the Austro-Hungarian flag. But not even these icy islands remained Austria’s for long. They later relinquished their claim to Russia. In the 1870s, Austria seemed to be on the verge of actually acquiring a colony. The businessman Gustav Freiherr von Overbeck had a plan to secure land in northeastern Borneo for the Habsburg Monarchy. Vienna showed interest and even sent a warship, the corvette Erzherzog Friedrich, to explore the area. However, the situation escalated. In 1875, a skirmish with local inhabitants occurred on the coast, and Vienna immediately lost interest.

In the following years, Austria continued to send ships around the world. In 1884, the corvette Helgoland explored West Africa without acquiring any land. At the same time, the Aurora traveled to South America to establish new trade relations. Africa also remained a focus. Between 1885 and 1887, the explorer Oscar Lenz led an expedition through the Congo River. They mapped large sections of the river, but again, no territorial claims arose. Perhaps the most dramatic episode followed in the Pacific. In 1896, the island of Guadalcanal was explored in search of raw materials such as nickel. The expedition ended in disaster. After a skirmish with locals in the island’s interior, several participants and the expedition leader were killed. A final attempt was made in China. At the end of the century, attention turned to East Asia.

In 1899, Austria dispatched the cruiser Kaiserin Elisabeth to China. The idea was to lease its own port, similar to what the German Empire had already done. But this came to nothing. After the suppression of the Boxer Rebellion, Austria-Hungary received only a small trading concession in 1901: a district in Tianjin, which lasted until 1917. A modest success, and also the last, because in 1917, in the midst of the First World War, Austria lost even this territory. Speaking of the First World War, there is one crucial territorial claim that must be added as the final point of Austrian colonial policy: Bosnia and Herzegovina. In 1878, Austria-Hungary occupied the territory, officially with the approval of the Congress of Berlin. While it formally remained under the sovereignty of the Ottoman Sultan, in practice Vienna assumed control, and that control extended far beyond normal administration. Bosnia and Herzegovina was systematically developed economically, its infrastructure expanded, and it was politically controlled, much like a classic colony. For this reason, historians often refer to it as an “internal colony. ”

Three decades later, the next step followed. In 1908, the territory was officially annexed and fully integrated into the monarchy. Even after this, however, its status remained unique. Bosnia and Herzegovina belonged neither to Austria nor to Hungary. Instead, it was administered directly by the joint Ministry of Finance of the Dual Monarchy, as a kind of separate administrative region within the empire. Bosnia and Herzegovina is thus the only territory where Austria-Hungary actually implemented anything resembling colonial structures. But not overseas, rather in the heart of Europe. With this action, the Habsburgs definitively annexed a territory that actually belonged to the Ottoman Empire, and above all, a region inhabited by many Serbs. The problem? Serbia saw itself as the protector of all Slavs, including the Serbs in Bosnia.

For Serbia, the annexation was a provocation and a direct loss of power in its goal of establishing a South Slavic state that was to include Bosnia and Herzegovina. Relations between Austria, Hungary, and Serbia became extremely strained after the annexation, and with the support of Russia for the Serbs and Germany for Austria, this regional conflict became a European risk that ultimately tipped the scales in favor of the outbreak of the First World War. So what impact did the colonial era have on the present? In short, Austria was indeed part of European colonialism. Not because it possessed a large colonial empire, but because it repeatedly attempted to build one. The failure of these attempts was primarily due to the geopolitical situation and the fact that other powers were simply faster and stronger. But just because Austria did not possess permanent overseas colonies does not mean it was uninvolved. Austria also benefited from colonial structures; goods from the colonies, such as coffee, sugar, and spices, had long been part of everyday life. And not only that. These connections also shaped the prevailing mindset. The idea of Europe as superior and other cultures as inferior was widespread at the time, even here. Therefore, it is clear that Austria cannot simply shirk its responsibility, as is often done today with the claim, “Well, we didn’t have any colonies.
” The effects of colonialism shaped all of Europe and did not stop at Austria’s borders.
